title: America's immigration policy is driving away future AI leaders
content:
The Trump administration has proposed a new fee for H-1B visas, while weighing a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training, the program that allows international graduates to work in the U.S. for one to three years after finishing their degrees. Roughly 419,000 people were working on OPT in 2024. For many of them, it was likely a major factor in choosing an American university over a school in Canada, the U.K., or Australia.
It is ironic that just weeks ago, headlines lamented the fact that one of the most talented international students we’ve seen in recent years chose to return to China, the U.S.’ biggest competitor. Yang Zhilin then went on to set up Moonshot AI, whose Kimi K3 open model has drawn comparisons to models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Why didn’t he build his company in the U.S.? After all, Yang got his Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. He interned at Google and Meta, and received a job offer from Apple. But Yang wanted to build his own company, and our visa system didn’t have a way to keep him here in the way that he wanted.
Some experts have proposed stapling a green card to every AI Ph.D. diploma — and they’re not wrong, but this idea and the OPT assume that the brightest minds want to work for our big tech companies first, then build after learning from the giants for several years. That’s not the case anymore.
Work experience isn’t as relevant when AI has flattened and accelerated everything. Founders are starting companies in their mid-20s — straight out of or even before finishing their Ph.D. The population capable of starting a frontier AI company is small, and more than two-thirds of these individuals are foreign. That cohort isn’t likely to want to spend five years or more in someone else’s company waiting for a green card, watching their idea age out.
40% The share of Nobel Prizes won by Americans in chemistry, medicine, and physics since 2000 that have gone to immigrants in the country.
And what does the U.S. do? It tightens and slows down its immigration system. In addition to the $100,000 for OPTs, the window for students to remain in the country after finishing a degree has been cut from 60 days to 30 to combat “rampant visa abuse.” Which means students will spend the last year of their Ph.D. stressing about finding a job quickly, instead of thinking about how to commercialize their ideas.
The Trump administration is also trying to end birthright citizenship, which is another draw for immigrants. Officials even floated the idea of barring foreign employees at U.S. labs from frontier-model access before the industry pushed back.
Other nations have taken notice of these actions, and are using them to their own advantage. Canada opened a program for U.S. H-1B holders and had to close it within a day since it was oversubscribed. Australia, France, and others are openly running recruitment campaigns aimed at researchers based in the U.S.
China spotted an opportunity even earlier: It launched the Thousand Talents Plan in 2008 and pulled back more than 7,000 people within a decade. China has recently increased funding for research while the U.S. has cut science funding, and that is proving to be a big incentive for some. Omar Yaghi, who was born into a refugee family in Jordan and came to the U.S. as a teenager to study, shared the Nobel Prize in chemistry last year. He recently left his faculty post at the University of California, Berkeley, for a position at Tsinghua University in Beijing, where he will lead an institute using AI to accelerate the discovery of new materials.
Yaghi was just one of many immigrant Nobel laureates in the U.S. Immigrants have been awarded 40% of the Nobel Prizes won by Americans in chemistry, medicine, and physics since 2000, according to a recent report by the National Foundation for American Policy, a research organization.
The high number of immigrant Nobel Prize winners reflects “a greater openness to immigration that has helped make the U.S. the leading global destination for research in many different science and technology fields, including computer and information sciences, cancer research and others,” the NFAP said.
If we persist in making it harder for international students to come to and stay in the U.S., this may no longer be true. Today, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, set up in 2022, will lend a company between $10 million and $150 million to build technologies deemed to be critical to national security. What we also need is an Office of Strategic Human Capital that can identify brilliant international AI students in critical fields and say, here is your long-term American visa, here is $10 million, go build.
In September, the U.S. and China are scheduled to hold talks on AI. Chip export control is sure to be a hot topic of discussion. What they will not admit is that you can’t export-control where a person decides to build a company. For decades, the U.S. was the first choice, but this is not the case anymore.
Immigration reform will take years, and the damage that is being done now will be hard to undo. For decades, for people like me and my family, immigration to the U.S. was a one-way door: You came, you stayed, you built here. The door swings both ways now. Yang Zhilin and Omar Yaghi are just the most visible examples of this. They will not be the last, and if the U.S. does not act, China will pull ahead in the race for AI talent.

report.summary: 美国收紧移民政策，正失去AI顶尖人才，中国等受益。
report.background: 特朗普政府拟对H-1B和OPT收费，缩短毕业留美窗口，甚至取消出生公民权，使国际学生留美创业更难。文章称，前沿AI人才中超过三分之二为外国人，但他们不愿为绿卡在大公司等待多年。与此同时，中国通过千人计划和资金吸引顶尖科学家回国，杨植麟创立Moonshot AI，杨培东离开伯克利去清华。美国移民贡献了40%诺贝尔奖，政策却反其道而行。
key_points: 美国拟对OPT收10万美元费用，毕业留美窗口从60天减至30天，国际学生留美门槛大幅提高。
前沿AI创业者趋于年轻化，不愿等待多年绿卡，更倾向直接创业，美国签证体系已不匹配。
中国等国家主动抢人，杨植麟和杨培东成为标志性案例，千人计划已吸引超7000人。
移民获得美国40%诺贝尔奖，是科技优势基石，当前政策正削弱这一基石。
report.impact: 对AI行业，美国可能失去下一代创新领袖，前沿模型研究优势下降，全球竞争格局向中国倾斜。对国际开发者，签证障碍迫使他们选择加拿大、欧洲或回国，职业路径改变。对普通用户，未来AI产品可能更多来自海外公司，技术中心转移。美国若不变革，损害难以逆转。
report.tools: 可关注Moonshot AI的开源模型Kimi K3，对比中美前沿大模型；跟踪NFAP移民与诺贝尔奖报告，了解人才趋势；留意各国人才引进项目动态。
